summary: 1932 Forest Service live-in lookout on the NC-TN line near Hot Springs; restored in 2018 by a partnership and reachable on the Appalachian Trail, unstaffed.

facts.design: 14 by 14 ft live-in cab with catwalk on a metal tower

access.note: Reached on foot by a short side trail, or by hiking the Appalachian Trail; a gravel road of about six miles from the Hot Springs side is usually closed in winter.

visit.trail_note: Small parking area near Tanyard Gap on US 25/70; the Appalachian Trail runs 2.4 miles north to the tower. The gravel road is about six miles long and is usually closed in winter.

events.note: Erected by the Forest Service with a 14-by-14-foot live-in cab.
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register, April 2, 2008.
Restored by a partnership of the Forest Service, ATC, FFLA and Carolina Mountain Club; ribbon cutting November 19, 2018.

evidence.supports: Location on the NC-TN line in the Pisgah National Forest, just off the Appalachian Trail
evidence.quote: Located on the NC/TN state line on the Pisgah National Forest, Rich Mountain Lookout is just off the Appalachian Trail.

evidence.supports: The live-in cab with catwalk is on a 30-foot metal tower
evidence.quote: The 14’x14’ live-in cab with catwalk is on a 30’ metal tower.

evidence.supports: The register records the tower as not staffed
evidence.quote: Staffed? No

evidence.supports: Erected by the Forest Service in 1932 with a 14-by-14-foot live-in cab
evidence.quote: The lookout tower was erected by the United States Forest Service in 1932, capped by a 14-by-14-foot live-in cab.

evidence.supports: Actively staffed until the 1990s and not live-in after the 1970s
evidence.quote: The tower was actively staffed until the 1990s, however, it ceased to be a live-in lookout in the 1970s.

evidence.supports: Aerial detection and later public phone reports proved more cost-effective and quicker
evidence.quote: Aerial detection by planes and later, reporting by the public via cell phones, became more cost effective and time efficient.

evidence.supports: Most North Carolina fire towers were taken down
evidence.quote: The majority of fire towers across North Carolina were dismantled.

evidence.supports: Weather and vandalism caused disrepair
evidence.quote: The tower at Rich Mountain had fallen into disrepair in recent years from stresses of weather extremes and vandalism.

evidence.supports: Partnership restored the tower in 2018
evidence.quote: In 2018, a partnership comprised of the US Forest Service, Appalachian Trail Conservancy, Forest Fire Lookout Association, and Carolina Mountain Club joined forces for a complete restoration.

evidence.supports: The travel guide credits much of the funding to the ATC license plate program
evidence.quote: Much of the funding came from the Appalachian Trail Conservancy’s (ATC) License Plate Grant Program

evidence.supports: A travel guide gives the tower as 31 feet and the route from Hot Springs
evidence.quote: To reach the 31-foot tall tower, drive US 25/70 east for 2.8 miles from Hot Springs.

evidence.supports: The gravel road is usually closed in winter
evidence.quote: The road is usually closed for winter months.

evidence.supports: Gravel road about six miles to the top
evidence.quote: Turn left on the gravel road and drive six miles up to the tower.

evidence.supports: Restoration by the Carolina Mountain Club, ATC, FFLA and Forest Service
evidence.quote: The historic Rich Mountain Fire Lookout Tower has been restored, thanks to a collaborative effort from the Carolina Mountain Club, the Appalachian Trail Conservancy, the Forest Fire Lookout Association and the U.S. Forest Service.

evidence.supports: Visitors can reach the tower by a short side trail
evidence.quote: accessible using a short side trail

evidence.quote: The Forest Fire Lookout Association contributed $1,000 and the Forest Service provided the bulk of funding, $101,158.

evidence.supports: License plate program amounts from North Carolina and Tennessee
evidence.quote: $3,500 from N.C. and $5,000 from Tennessee.

evidence.supports: A Forest Service fire officer spoke about once acting as lookout in the tower
evidence.quote: of his time acting as lookout in the very tower under which he was speaking

evidence.quote: November 19, 2018: A ribbon cutting ceremony was held to recognize the years of hard work and dedication

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register gives a 30-foot metal tower and Romantic Asheville gives 31 feet. The story says about 30 feet and mentions both; facts use 9.1 m (30 ft).

Romantic Asheville says much of the funding came from the ATC license plate program. Smoky Mountain News gives the Forest Service the bulk ($101,158) and the two states' plate programs $8,500 combined. The story follows the newspaper's figures.

sources.title: Rich Mountain Lookout Fire Tower, Hot Springs
Restored Fire Tower Harkens Back To Bygone Era

notes_for_editor: Build year (1932), location and the 2018 restoration agree across sources. Unverified leads not used: a search summary says public access ended in 2017, and another says a CCC camp manned the tower from 1933; neither appeared in a page I opened. Elevation: the register and Smoky Mountain News give 3,670 ft (1,119 m, matching the brief's 1118.6 m); Romantic Asheville gives 3,643 ft. No post-2018 condition report was found; the travel guide calls the tower in excellent condition but is undated, so verify the current state before relying on access.
